Artificial intelligence is reshaping nearly every technical field, from software engineering and mathematics to materials discovery. That raises a direct question for our own discipline: how can AI expand what is possible in computer systems and chip design? Modern systems are growing harder to build just as the demand for specialized silicon accelerates. Designing a competitive computer system requires coordinating choices across workloads, compilers, instruction sets, microarchitectures, and physical layout, where decisions in one layer constrain every other. Because learned methods can guide searches through large design spaces, fit empirical patterns where analytical models fall short, and propose candidate structures a designer would not have drafted by hand, they open the possibility of exploring cross-layer architectural trade-offs that manual workflows rarely have time to consider.

At the same time, computer systems and silicon put those capabilities to an unusually hard test. An architectural decision begins with high-level software intent and cascades through compilers, instruction set architectures, microarchitectures, and register-transfer level (RTL) netlists down to physical signoff. Every measurement along that path is expensive, noisy, and partial, because compilers, cycle-level simulators, formal verification engines, and post-layout timing tools each expose only a narrow slice of system behavior and their assumptions often conflict. In hardware, the cost of an error is also asymmetric. While software can often be patched after deployment, a timing glitch or coherence bug discovered after tapeout may require revised masks and another pass through fabrication if firmware updates or operating limits cannot contain it. Such respins remain common; in the 2024 Wilson Research Group study, only 14 percent of surveyed integrated-circuit projects achieved first-silicon success [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024].

That high cost of error is both the danger and the opportunity of automated design. Earlier computer architecture practice, *Architecture 1.0*, was built around human architects. Hardware description languages, cycle-level simulators, and modular design flows were developed to help people explore alternatives, reason about trade-offs, and make decisions. *Architecture 2.0* asks what changes when automated agents and search loops begin proposing and revising architectural decisions themselves. Building that capability takes far more than a better standalone model. Generative models and optimizers can draft candidate RTL and microarchitectural variations far faster than physical toolchains can evaluate them, yet generating more candidates helps only if we can test what they actually do in silicon. An *AI-native design system* rebuilds the exploration loop around the data, baselines, verification methods, and evaluation frameworks that return physical evidence, connecting learned surrogates, cycle-level simulators, and signoff engines through shared design records so that hardware and software trade-offs can be explored systematically within a clear verification budget.

Three years ago, when Amir Yazdanbakhsh and I wrote an ACM SIGARCH blog post calling for an "Architecture 2.0" AI gymnasium [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2023Gymnasium] and helped convene our first community workshop [@Architecture20SIGARCHWorkshopOutcomes], the idea of prompting a design system to carry a high-level workload request through to a verified chip sounded to many like an outlandish moonshot, almost a ridiculous prompt. Even as we developed the framework in our subsequent paper [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20], the proposal met with candid skepticism across the computer architecture community. The hard part of building a computer was never simply generating a snippet of code; it was deciding what to build, carrying exploration across architectural boundaries as physical feedback returned, and knowing when the result could be trusted.

In the years since that initial post, what once sounded far-fetched has become an active research frontier. Commercial reinforcement-learning optimizers had already entered block-level implementation workflows [@Synopsys2023DSOai], and since then research and industry teams have demonstrated learned macro placement, model-assisted RTL drafting, automated kernel generation, and early multi-agent tool harnesses. Even so, a wave of isolated ideas and point tools does not by itself make a coherent design methodology. Extending exploration across subsystem boundaries still requires coordinating tool assumptions, revisiting hardware and software interfaces together, and holding every candidate to rigorous physical checks.

This book looks beyond isolated point assistance and bounded subsystem tuning to ask whether a complete, closed-loop design system can find better architectures, cut the engineering cost of finding them, or do both. I wrote it to bring these emerging pieces together into a single engineering discipline, making the moonshot concrete without assuming it will succeed. Across the chapters that follow, the architectural problem always comes first. Depending on the physical constraints, the right choice for a given problem may combine learned surrogates, heuristic search, formal proofs, or conventional analysis with no machine learning at all. Architecture 2.0 does not claim that every circuit needs an AI model; it names both the shift toward closed-loop, cross-stack exploration and the discipline of holding AI-native design systems to an architecture-grade evidence standard, where the first question is always where AI earns its place and what physical evidence its recommendations must deliver.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

To judge whether an automated workflow improves a design program, an architect has to examine the whole system of people and tools rather than a single model in isolation. A fluent generative model inside a broken verification loop only produces invalid silicon faster, whereas a modest, well-calibrated surrogate that removes a weeks-long simulation bottleneck can change a tapeout schedule. Every method in this book therefore faces two questions: *did the complete approach improve the architecture result, or reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable one, against a credible alternative?* And *should a named authority commit physical silicon to the result?* The first question is technical and measurable; the second is an organizational judgment that a human architect makes and owns.

Three practical moves across the chapters ahead answer both questions: formulating the architecture question and recording the design state clearly enough for tools to use, connecting search methods to real simulators and signoff engines while checking what those tools return, and evaluating the complete workflow before deciding whether to commit. A single engineering team can apply all three moves with the tools it already has, before the final chapter widens the lens to ask which remaining bottlenecks require shared community infrastructure.

A recurring case study makes these ideas concrete across every chapter: the Lighthouse study, a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem designed for a strict 3\ W thermal design power budget and tight die-area limits. The Lighthouse study is prospective, tracing an architectural hypothesis through the exact evidence an engineering claim would require. It begins by framing the 3\ W design question in @sec-moonshot, organizes the study's life cycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, builds a structured record of the design state in @sec-data-representations-world-models, and shows in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces which tool interfaces and verification checks must be in place before an automated cache study can even be dispatched. Alongside that prospective thread, a companion systolic-array study runs a complete, pre-registered simulator comparison on synthetic matrix-multiplication kernels; the simulator measurements are examined in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust, and the tied candidate and its transposition probe are tested against a workload shift in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack. Neither study on its own settles the full Lighthouse subsystem, whose power budget, accelerator, memory traffic, and thermal behavior would still have to be verified together; both records return in @sec-what-architect-owns, where the book applies its own evidence standard to those results and states what work remains before silicon commitment.

Carrying a study like that from high-level intent to physical evidence requires drawing on computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation (EDA; @fig-book-composition). Each pairwise overlap already has a substantial body of work behind it: architecture and machine learning help us predict performance and search large design spaces, architecture and EDA connect system choices to RTL and physical layout, and machine learning and EDA are already reshaping synthesis, placement, routing, and verification. What we are after sits where all three meet.

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture defines the workload questions and system trade-offs, machine learning provides methods for prediction, generation, and search, and EDA supplies the synthesis, layout, and verification tools that ground candidate designs in physical measurements.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="100%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection."}

At that three-way intersection, a study has to answer to the evidence standards of all three fields at once. A generated artifact that ignores the workload is not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive layout and timing closure is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair baseline comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

Because the required evidence depends on how much of the workflow is automated, @sec-moonshot distinguishes three operational layers: helping an engineer with an isolated task, tuning a subsystem within fixed interfaces, and searching across hardware and software boundaries toward verified silicon. This book is not a catalog of neural network architectures, a prompt-engineering recipe, or a defense of unchecked autonomy. Physical signoff checks remain decisive, and named human architects remain accountable for every committed tapeout.

## The Discipline of Design Principles {.unnumbered}

Machine-learning models, EDA scripts, and the prompts and wrappers written around them go stale within months. What lasts is an engineering principle rooted in semiconductor physics, the cost of a measurement, and documented failure modes. A durable architectural principle will still govern the silicon outcome even if model capability grows by orders of magnitude and inference cost falls to zero. A team that grounds its automated workflow in clear problem formulation, explicit state records, tool discipline, fair baseline comparisons, and human signoff authority can adopt each new generation of models without rebuilding its methodology.

Each principle in this book appears alongside the technical problem that calls for it, summarized in design-principle callouts that pair the rule with how to apply it in practice, while @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes gathers the foundational laws and paradoxes they build on as a quick reference. Because those principles connect hardware physics, design automation, and machine learning, they are written to serve readers across all three communities.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect, chip designer, and systems researcher. The book assumes familiarity with performance, power, area, and hardware–software interfaces, along with working literacy in engineering software (Python, C++, or a standard hardware description language). No background in deep learning is required; the machine-learning ideas the argument needs are introduced where they are used, through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Because Architecture 2.0 draws on fields that have mostly worked apart, the book is written for four technical communities:

- **Computer architects** who want to bring automated search and generative models into design exploration without loosening the physical checks that make a result trustworthy.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification toolchains to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to see how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification change what counts as a valid result.
- **Graduate students and engineering leaders** working across hardware and software who need a practical framework and shared vocabulary for governing AI-native systems engineering.

## How to Read This Book {#book-structure .unnumbered}

The eleven chapters build cumulatively and follow an architectural study from initial intent through evaluation to the final commitment decision:

- @sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, and @sec-architecture-20-ontology set out the moonshot and its evidence standard, analyze the physical scaling limits and economic pressures straining manual design loops, and introduce the six-stage design life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit) through the running Lighthouse mobile XR study.
- @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, and @sec-feedback-verification-trust build the core engineering machinery of Architecture 2.0: recording the design state in structured representations, choosing the simplest method that fits the bottleneck, wrapping simulators and EDA flows in reproducible tool harnesses, and checking what those tools return before acting on it.
- @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, and @sec-what-architect-owns examine how closed-loop patterns transfer across the stack, how to test complete workflows under matched budgets and adversarial red-teaming, and why a human architect remains responsible for the final signoff decision.
- @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem charts the shared schemas, open benchmarks, grand challenges, and university curricula needed to sustain an open research ecosystem.

Although reading the chapters in order gives the complete engineering argument, each of the four communities above can also enter through the chapters closest to its own work (@tbl-reading-paths). Three chapters form the spine every path shares: the moonshot and its evidence standard (@sec-moonshot), the life cycle that organizes the work (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), and the commitment decision that closes it (@sec-what-architect-owns).

| **Reader** | **Start with** | **Then** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Computer architect | @sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-what-architect-owns |
| EDA and CAD engineer | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack |
| Machine learning researcher | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect |
| Graduate student or engineering leader | @sec-moonshot, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, @sec-what-architect-owns, @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem |
: **Four reading paths tailored to each technical community.** EDA developers and ML researchers gain most from starting with state representations and execution harnesses, whereas architects and engineering leaders gain most from focusing on cross-stack transfer, workflow evaluation, and signoff ownership. {#tbl-reading-paths tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

As you read, test these principles against a live design problem in your own work. Ask which decision matters, which hidden physical constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what the tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. The measure of this book is whether its principles carry to design problems it never mentions.

Artificial intelligence is likely to change how architects design chips and systems. Whether it does depends on our discipline taking that prospect seriously without taking anyone's claims on faith, this book's included. Generating code is not that change. The change, if it comes, will come from design systems that carry intent to checked physical results and from architects with the judgment to govern them.
